lessons.title: Where did it go?

blocks.text: Choose a positive direction
Position is measured from a chosen origin. With right positive, displacement is final position minus initial position. A move from 2 m to 9 m has displacement +7 m; the sign records its direction.
Return to the start

The length of a trip counts every part of the path. Returning to the starting position gives zero displacement even though the object has travelled. Follow the dot out and back before comparing the endpoints.
Move the origin
Changing the origin changes both position readings by the same amount. Their difference stays the same. The physical trip does not become longer when you rename the starting coordinate.
Count a reversal
A reversal creates another stretch of travel. From 0 m to 8 m and then back to 3 m, the distance is 8 + 5 = 13 m. The displacement uses only the endpoints: +3 m.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish a change in position from the total distance travelled.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Speed and direction

blocks.text: How much each second?

Average speed divides total distance by elapsed time. Travelling 18 m in 6 s gives 3 m/s. That average describes the whole interval; it does not establish that the object moved equally fast at every moment.
Keep the direction
Average velocity divides signed displacement by elapsed time. A displacement of −12 m over 3 s gives −4 m/s. Speed uses a magnitude, so a negative velocity still describes positive speed.
One trip, two averages
A return trip can have zero average velocity. The final position equals the initial position, so their difference is zero. Average speed still counts the full distance travelled during the interval.
Combine unequal times

To average a whole trip, divide its total distance by its total time. Travelling 6 m in 2 s and another 6 m in 4 s gives 12/6 = 2 m/s. An ordinary average of the two speeds would give the wrong weighting.

lessons.orientation: Use elapsed time to distinguish average speed from average velocity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Read a motion graph

blocks.text: The slope tells a rate
A position–time graph puts time on the horizontal axis. Along a straight segment, divide the position change by the time change to get velocity. From 2 m to 14 m in 3 s, that slope is +4 m/s.
A flat line is a pause
A horizontal segment holds the same position while time passes. Its velocity is zero. The graph represents position over time, so a flat segment is a pause rather than a picture of a level road.
A downward slope
A downward segment means position decreases as time increases. With right positive, that is leftward velocity. It does not mean the object is below the ground or falling through the page.
Read the whole interval

For average velocity over several segments, use the overall endpoints. The pause and reversal still contribute elapsed time. Moving from 0 m to 2 m over 6 s gives an average velocity of one-third of a metre per second.

lessons.orientation: Interpret a position–time graph as changing position, pauses and reversals.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Changing velocity

blocks.text: Change per second
Acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes. Going from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s gives (10 − 2)/4 = 2 m/s². With constant acceleration, equal time intervals add equal changes in velocity.
A positive acceleration can slow you
Signs describe directions. A leftward cart changing from −8 m/s to −2 m/s has positive acceleration because its velocity increases. Its speed falls from 8 m/s to 2 m/s.
Compare velocity and acceleration
When velocity and acceleration point in the same direction, speed increases. A cart already moving left speeds up under a leftward acceleration. A minus sign by itself does not mean slowing down.
Constant velocity
A horizontal velocity–time graph has zero slope. Its acceleration is zero, although the cart can still move. Position continues to change while a nonzero velocity stays constant.

lessons.orientation: Read acceleration as a signed change in velocity per second.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Predict the next position

blocks.text: Add the velocity change
For constant acceleration, final velocity is initial velocity plus acceleration times elapsed time: v = u + at. Starting at 3 m/s and adding 2 m/s each second gives 11 m/s after 4 s.
The area under velocity

With constant acceleration, average velocity is halfway between the initial and final velocities. Multiply that average by time to find displacement. The same result follows from displacement = ut + ½at².
Twice the time
Starting from rest with constant acceleration gives displacement = ½at². Doubling the duration multiplies displacement by four. The object covers more ground each second as it picks up speed.
Predict a stop

A cart starting at 12 m/s with acceleration −3 m/s² reaches zero velocity after 4 s. During that interval its average velocity is 6 m/s, so its stopping distance is 24 m. End the braking model at the stop.

lessons.orientation: Use a constant acceleration to predict velocity and displacement.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Falling and rising

blocks.text: Choose upward as positive

In this model, gravitational acceleration is 10 m/s² downward and air resistance is absent. With upward positive, acceleration is −10 m/s². A released ball gains downward velocity even though it starts at rest.
Height is a position
A falling object's displacement is negative when upward is positive. Add that signed displacement to its initial height. From 45 m, falling for 2 s changes height by −20 m, leaving a height of 25 m.
At the top

An upward throw has positive initial velocity and negative acceleration. At its highest point, velocity is momentarily zero. Gravity still acts downward, so acceleration is not zero and the ball begins to descend.
What the model leaves out

Free fall here means gravity acts without air resistance. At the same location, objects released together from the same height share the same gravitational acceleration, regardless of mass. Shape-dependent drag would require a different model.

lessons.orientation: Apply constant downward acceleration to free fall and an upward throw.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: When forces balance

blocks.text: Combine the pushes
Choose the object before adding forces. For right positive, a 14 N rightward force and a 6 N leftward force give a net force of +8 N. Equal arrows in opposite directions would sum to zero.
Motion without a net push

With zero net force, velocity stays constant. A moving cart can keep travelling while its forces balance. Newton's first law describes unchanged velocity, including the special case of remaining at rest.
Rest is one possibility
If an object starts at rest and its forces stay balanced, it remains at rest. Balanced does not mean no forces act: an opposing pair on the same object can have a zero sum.
The larger force sets the result
The net force points toward the larger opposing force. A cart moving right can have a leftward net force; the force changes its velocity rather than reporting the direction it already travels.

lessons.orientation: Add signed forces and distinguish balanced forces from being at rest.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Force, mass and acceleration

blocks.text: Divide the net force
Newton's second law connects net force, mass and acceleration: F_net = ma. A 3 kg cart with 18 N right and 6 N left has net force 12 N, so its acceleration is 12/3 = 4 m/s² rightward.
Change the mass

The same net force gives less acceleration to a larger mass. Doubling mass halves acceleration when the force stays fixed. Mass measures resistance to a change in velocity; it does not specify the current speed.
Change the force
For the same mass, acceleration changes in proportion to the net force. A 2 kg cart under 24 N accelerates at 12 m/s². Compare its motion with the same cart under 12 N.
An opposing net force

The sign of acceleration follows the net force. With right positive, forces of 4 N right and 12 N left on a 4 kg cart give acceleration −2 m/s². A rightward-moving cart initially slows under this acceleration.

lessons.orientation: Use net force and mass to predict how velocity changes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Weight and support

blocks.text: Mass is not weight
Weight is the gravitational force on an object: magnitude W = mg. Mass is measured in kilograms; weight is measured in newtons. In a field with g = 10 m/s², a 3 kg object weighs 30 N.
Change the gravitational field
Moving to a different gravitational field changes weight without changing mass. The same 3 kg object weighs 30 N where g = 10 m/s² and 4.8 N where g = 1.6 m/s².
Resting on a support
When only weight and an upward support force act, zero vertical acceleration requires them to balance. A 4 kg object at rest with g = 10 m/s² has a 40 N upward support force.
A support can push harder
An upward acceleration requires a net upward force. With upward positive, N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a). A 4 kg object accelerating upward at 2 m/s² where g = 10 m/s² needs support force 48 N.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish mass, gravitational force and the force from a support.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Forces come in pairs

blocks.text: Name both objects

When A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal force in the opposite direction. These forces act on different objects. If B pushes A left with 10 N, A pushes B right with 10 N, even when their masses differ.
Equal forces, different motion

The interaction forces have equal magnitudes, but acceleration also depends on mass. Under the 10 N interaction, a 5 kg cart accelerates at 2 m/s² while a 2 kg cart accelerates at 5 m/s² in the opposite direction.
Keep the direction
Choose right as positive for both carts. Cart A experiences a leftward force, so its acceleration is negative. For a 2 kg cart with force −10 N, acceleration is −5 m/s².
Choose the system

The two forces do not cancel on either cart: each cart accelerates. They do cancel when adding internal forces for the combined A-and-B system. That cancellation does not remove any external force on the system.

lessons.orientation: Identify an interaction pair and explain why equal forces can produce different accelerations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Friction that adjusts

blocks.text: Before the box moves

Static friction adjusts to oppose the tendency to slide, up to a limit. For a 4 kg box with g = 10 m/s² and static coefficient 0.5, that limit is 20 N. A 12 N push is balanced by 12 N of static friction.
Beyond the limit

On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the support force is mg. Maximum static friction is μ_s mg. A push above that maximum starts sliding; static friction is not automatically at its maximum before then.
While it slides
For this ideal model, sliding friction has magnitude μ_k mg and opposes sliding. With mass 4 kg, g = 10 m/s² and μ_k = 0.3, its magnitude is 12 N. It need not match the applied push.
Subtract the opposing force

A sliding 4 kg box pushed right with 24 N has 12 N of sliding friction left. Net force is 12 N, so acceleration is 3 m/s². With the push removed it slows; friction does not launch it backward after it stops.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish static and sliding friction, and predict whether a push moves a box.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: When a force does work

blocks.text: Force along a displacement
A constant force does positive work when it acts along the displacement. Work is force times displacement in that direction: W = Fd. A 15 N force acting along a 4 m displacement does 60 J of work.
Force against a displacement

A force opposite to displacement does negative work. A 6 N friction force acting against 5 m of travel does −30 J. The sign describes the force's energy transfer, not whether the object exists to the left or right.
A perpendicular force
Only the component of force along displacement contributes to work. A perpendicular support force does zero work during a horizontal displacement, even though the force is nonzero.
Track the chosen force
Work is calculated for a particular force. A 10 N pull along 7 m does 70 J, while a separate opposing 4 N force would do −28 J over the same displacement. Adding all the forces' work gives net work.

lessons.orientation: Calculate signed work for forces along, against and perpendicular to displacement.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Energy of motion

blocks.text: Energy carried by motion
Kinetic energy is K = ½mv². For a 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s, K = 9 J. The squared speed makes fast motion costly to stop: doubling speed changes energy more than doubling mass.
Speed is squared
At fixed mass, twice the speed gives four times the kinetic energy. Compare the bars for the same cart at 3 m/s and 6 m/s. The energy grows by 2², not by 2.
Mass is a direct multiplier
At fixed speed, doubling mass doubles kinetic energy. Kinetic energy is nonnegative and depends on speed; it is the same for equal speeds in opposite directions.
Net work changes kinetic energy
The work-energy theorem states W_net = K_final − K_initial. Speeding a 2 kg cart from 3 m/s to 5 m/s changes its kinetic energy from 9 J to 25 J, requiring net work of 16 J.

lessons.orientation: Use kinetic energy and net work to connect force with a change in speed.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Energy and height

blocks.text: A change of height
Near Earth's surface, with constant g, gravitational potential-energy change is ΔU = mgΔh. Raising a 3 kg object from 1 m to 5 m where g = 10 m/s² increases this energy by 120 J.
Choose a reference

A height reference sets where U = 0. Shifting the reference changes the heights assigned to both endpoints but leaves their difference unchanged. The same physical rise has the same potential-energy change.
A descent has a negative change
Falling lowers gravitational potential energy. For mass 2 kg and g = 10 m/s², moving from 8 m to 3 m gives Δh = −5 m and ΔU = −100 J. The lost potential energy can become motion or heating.
Gravity does the opposite work
Work done by gravity is −ΔU. When a 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s², gravity does +100 J of work. A slow lifting force instead adds energy while gravity does negative work.

lessons.orientation: Calculate gravitational potential-energy changes using a chosen height reference.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Where the energy goes

blocks.text: Follow the energy

Consider the object, Earth and track together, with no energy entering or leaving. With no heating, a 2 kg object released from height 10 m at g = 10 m/s² converts 200 J of gravitational potential energy into 200 J of kinetic energy at zero height.
Include heating
Friction can turn mechanical energy into thermal energy. If the same descent produces 40 J of heating, final kinetic energy is 200 − 40 = 160 J. The energy has changed form; it has not disappeared.
Keep the boundary in view

For this closed system, kinetic plus gravitational potential plus thermal energy stays constant. Mechanical energy alone, K + U, decreases when heating increases. This model assigns heating progressively along the descent; its slider represents progress, not physical time.
Recover the speed

Kinetic energy determines speed through v = √(2K/m). After a 2 kg object loses 200 J of potential energy and 100 J becomes heating, its final kinetic energy is 100 J. Its speed is √(2 × 100 / 2) = 10 m/s.

lessons.orientation: Account for motion, height and heating during a descent.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Power and efficiency

blocks.text: Energy per second
Average power is energy transferred divided by time. A device delivering 1,200 J of useful energy in 4 s has useful output power 300 W. A watt is one joule per second.
Useful output as a fraction

Efficiency compares useful output energy with input energy. Here 1,200 J of useful output from 2,000 J input gives 1,200/2,000 = 0.6, or 60%. Efficiency compares energies over the same operating interval.
The remaining energy

Input energy must be accounted for. In a device with no net energy storage, the difference between input and useful output reaches other outputs such as heating or sound. Here that difference is 2,000 − 1,200 = 800 J.
Same job, different rate

Delivering the same useful energy in half the time doubles average useful power. It does not by itself improve efficiency: that also depends on input energy. Keep energy, time and useful fraction separate.

lessons.orientation: Separate energy transferred, transfer rate and the fraction reaching a useful output.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Momentum and impulse

blocks.text: Motion with a direction
Linear momentum is p = mv. A 3 kg cart moving right at 4 m/s has momentum +12 kg·m/s when right is positive. Unlike kinetic energy, one-dimensional momentum has a sign that records direction.
Force over time
For constant net force, impulse is J = FΔt. It equals the change in momentum. A 6 N net force to the right acting for 3 s adds +18 N·s of impulse, the same as +18 kg·m/s of momentum change.
From impulse to velocity
Add impulse to the initial momentum, then divide by mass. For a 3 kg cart initially at 4 m/s, a +18 N·s impulse changes momentum from 12 to 30 kg·m/s and final velocity becomes 10 m/s.
A reversal changes momentum

Equal speeds in opposite directions give equal kinetic energies but opposite momenta. Reversing a 2 kg cart from +4 to −4 m/s changes momentum by −16 kg·m/s, even though its initial and final speeds are equal.

lessons.orientation: Track signed momentum and use force acting over time to predict its change.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: When carts stick together

blocks.text: Choose both carts

During a brief collision with negligible external impulse, total momentum of the two-cart system stays constant. If they stick, both share one final velocity: v = (m_Au_A + m_Bu_B)/(m_A + m_B). Keep each cart's own mass attached to its own velocity.
Opposite momenta can balance

Choose right as positive before adding momenta. A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s and a 4 kg cart at −3 m/s have total momentum 12 − 12 = 0. If they stick with negligible external impulse, their shared final velocity is zero.
Momentum is not kinetic energy

A sticking collision conserves total momentum under the stated condition, but converts kinetic energy into deformation, thermal energy and sound. For a 2 kg cart at 6 m/s striking a resting 4 kg cart, initial kinetic energy is 36 J and final kinetic energy is 12 J.
Check the system boundary

The collision forces are internal to the two-cart system and cancel in its total momentum change. A significant external impulse would change total momentum. We assume that external impulse is negligible during the brief contact, not that every force is absent.

lessons.orientation: Conserve signed momentum across a sticking collision and account for the kinetic-energy change.

questions.prompt: An object moves from x = 2 m to x = 9 m. With right positive, what is its displacement in metres?
hints: Locate the starting and finishing coordinates.
Subtract the start from the finish.
Calculate 9 − 2.

questions.prompt: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What total distance does it travel, in metres?
hints: Count both stretches of the trip.
Each stretch has length 7 − 1 metres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It travels 6 m out and 6 m back, for 12 m.

questions.prompt: The origin shifts so that a trip from 2 m to 9 m is recorded as 12 m to 19 m. What happens to the displacement?
hints: Compare the differences between the two pairs of endpoints.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both readings increase by 10 m; their difference stays +7 m.

questions.prompt: A robot moves from 0 m to 8 m, then back to 3 m. How far does it travel altogether, in metres?
hints: Break the trip at the turning point.
The return stretch runs from 8 m to 3 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The path has lengths 8 m and 5 m: 8 + 5 = 13 m.

questions.prompt: A lift's marked position changes from 5 m to −4 m. With upward positive, find its displacement in metres.
hints: Keep the minus sign on the final position.
Subtract the initial position from the final position.
Calculate −4 − 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Final minus initial gives −4 − 5 = −9 m, downward.

questions.prompt: A cart travels from −2 m to 4 m and then to 1 m. Which statement describes its trip?
hints: Use endpoints for displacement and both path lengths for distance.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its displacement is 1 − (−2) = 3 m. Its distance is 6 + 3 = 9 m.

questions.prompt: A rover covers 18 m in 6 s without reversing. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Use total distance and elapsed time.
Divide distance by time.
Share the travelled distance equally across the elapsed seconds.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −12 m over 3 s. Find its average velocity in m/s.
hints: Velocity keeps the direction of displacement.
Divide the signed displacement by elapsed time.
Divide the displacement magnitude by duration and keep its negative sign.

questions.prompt: A runner goes 10 m from a marker and returns to that marker in a total of 5 s. Find the average velocity in m/s.
hints: Use the final and initial positions.
A return to the same point leaves no displacement.
Divide that displacement by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0/5 = 0 m/s.

questions.prompt: A robot travels 6 m in 2 s, then 6 m in 4 s. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
hints: Combine distances and times before dividing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s, giving 2 m/s. The slower section lasts longer.

questions.prompt: A conveyor moves a parcel 42 m along a straight path in 7 s. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Identify the path length and duration.
Use distance divided by time.
Find how many metres correspond to one second.

questions.prompt: A moving object returns to its start. Which average must be zero over the complete trip?
hints: Ask which average uses displacement.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only average velocity must be zero, because displacement is zero. The distance travelled is positive.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time segment goes from 2 m at 0 s to 14 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Read the changes on both axes.
Divide position change by time change.
Calculate (14 − 2)/3.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph is horizontal from 2 s to 4 s. What does the object do during that interval?
hints: Compare the position at the ends of the horizontal segment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position stays fixed during the interval, so the object is stationary.

choices.label: Moves at a positive constant speed

questions.prompt: Position falls from 10 m to 2 m along a straight graph segment lasting 4 s. Find the velocity in m/s.
hints: A falling position reading has a negative change.
Use final position minus initial position.
Calculate (2 − 10)/4.

questions.prompt: A graph starts at 0 m at 0 s and finishes at 2 m at 6 s, with a pause and reversal between. Find the overall average velocity in m/s; a fraction is accepted.
hints: Use the outer endpoints for the full interval.
Include the entire elapsed time, including the pause.
Divide 2 by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overall displacement is 2 m over 6 s: 2/6 = 1/3 m/s.

questions.prompt: A straight graph segment runs from x = 3 m at t = 1 s to x = 15 m at t = 4 s. Find its velocity in m/s.
hints: Subtract the earlier reading from the later reading on each axis.
Subtract the earlier time from the later time.
Divide the change in position by the change in time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Position change is 12 m and time change is 3 s: 12/3 = 4 m/s.

questions.prompt: What does a straight rising line on a position–time graph indicate?
hints: A graph of position against time shows a rate, not the shape of the road.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal time intervals produce equal positive position changes, which is constant positive velocity.

questions.prompt: A cart changes velocity from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Find the signed change in velocity.
Divide that change by the elapsed time.
Subtract initial from final velocity, then divide by duration.

questions.prompt: Velocity changes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s over 3 s. What is the average acceleration in m/s²?
hints: Subtract the initial negative velocity carefully.
The velocity moves toward zero.
Calculate (−2 − (−8))/3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The velocity change is −2 − (−8) = +6 m/s. Dividing by 3 s gives +2 m/s².

questions.prompt: A cart has negative velocity and negative acceleration. What happens to its speed while those signs remain?
hints: Compare the directions, rather than interpreting a minus sign as braking.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Velocity and acceleration both point left, so the magnitude of velocity increases.

questions.prompt: A cart keeps a velocity of 6 m/s for 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Acceleration depends on a change in velocity.
Compare the initial and final velocities.
Calculate (6 − 6)/4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is no velocity change: (6 − 6)/4 = 0 m/s².

questions.prompt: A robot's velocity changes from 9 m/s to −3 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: The final velocity points opposite to the initial velocity.
Keep signs when subtracting.
Divide the negative velocity change by elapsed time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is −3 − 9 = −12 m/s. Acceleration is −12/4 = −3 m/s².

questions.prompt: A velocity–time line crosses zero with a nonzero slope. At that instant, which description is possible?
hints: Velocity is the graph's height; acceleration is its slope.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The graph's value is zero at the crossing, while its slope remains nonzero.

choices.label: Zero velocity must mean zero acceleration

questions.prompt: A cart starts at 3 m/s and has constant acceleration 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find the velocity added during the interval.
Multiply acceleration by time, then add the initial velocity.
Calculate 3 + 2 × 4.

questions.prompt: Starting at 3 m/s, a cart accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: Account for both the initial motion and the added velocity.
Use ut + ½at² for constant acceleration.
Calculate 3 × 4 + 0.5 × 2 × 16.

questions.prompt: An object starts from rest with constant nonzero acceleration. Doubling the travel time multiplies its displacement by what factor?
hints: Track the exponent on time in ½at².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Displacement is proportional to time squared; doubling time gives a factor of 2² = 4.

questions.prompt: A cart brakes uniformly from 12 m/s to rest in 4 s. Find its stopping distance in metres.
hints: Uniform braking makes the velocity change linearly.
Average the initial and final velocities.
Multiply (12 + 0)/2 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Average velocity is (12 + 0)/2 = 6 m/s. Displacement is 6 × 4 = 24 m.

questions.prompt: A robot begins at x = 5 m with velocity 2 m/s and constant acceleration 1 m/s². Find its position after 4 s, in metres.
hints: First find displacement, then add the initial position.
Use x = x₀ + ut + ½at².
Calculate 5 + 8 + 8.

questions.prompt: When is displacement = ut + ½at² valid for the whole interval?
hints: Identify the assumption used to combine the velocity changes.

acceptedIdeas: When acceleration is constant over the interval
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This expression assumes constant acceleration during the interval; direction alone is not enough.

choices.label: When acceleration is constant over the interval

questions.prompt: A ball is released from rest. Take upward as positive and g = 10 m/s², with no air resistance. Find its velocity after 2 s, in m/s.
hints: Gravity points opposite to the positive direction.
Use negative acceleration in v = u + at.
Calculate 0 − 10 × 2.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from height 45 m. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, what is its height after 2 s, in metres?
hints: Find the downward displacement from rest.
Subtract ½gt² from the starting height.
Calculate 45 − 0.5 × 10 × 4.

questions.prompt: At the highest point of a vertical throw, find the acceleration in m/s². Take upward positive, g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance.
hints: Separate zero velocity from zero acceleration.
Gravity continues acting throughout the flight.
Use the downward value of g with upward positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Gravity still gives acceleration −10 m/s² at the top; only the instantaneous velocity is zero.

questions.prompt: Two objects of different mass are released together from the same height in the same gravitational field. Ignore air resistance. Which lands first?
hints: Check whether mass appears in the free-fall position equation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same initial velocity and gravitational acceleration give the same motion in this model.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upward at 30 m/s. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, find its displacement after 2 s in metres.
hints: Combine the initial upward motion with the downward acceleration.
Use ut − ½gt².
Calculate 60 − 20.

questions.prompt: While a freely thrown ball is moving upward, which direction does its acceleration point? Ignore air resistance.
hints: The direction of motion does not determine the direction of gravitational acceleration.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gravitational acceleration points downward throughout the flight, including while velocity points upward.

choices.label: Upward, because the ball is rising
It has no acceleration until it falls

questions.prompt: Two horizontal forces act on a cart: 14 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Give opposite directions opposite signs.
Add the signed forces on the same cart.
Calculate 14 − 6.

questions.prompt: A cart is already moving right at 3 m/s. Its net force stays zero. What happens next in an inertial frame?
hints: Balanced forces imply no change in velocity.

acceptedIdeas: It continues at 3 m/s to the right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero net force leaves the velocity unchanged.

choices.label: It continues at 3 m/s to the right

questions.prompt: A resting cart has 9 N rightward and 9 N leftward horizontal forces. Find its horizontal net force in newtons.
hints: Compare the two force magnitudes.
Use opposite signs for opposite directions.
Calculate 9 − 9.

questions.prompt: A cart moving right experiences 8 N right and 20 N left. With right positive, find the net force in newtons.
hints: Separate the velocity direction from the force sum.
The leftward force enters with a minus sign.
Calculate 8 − 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 20 = −12 N. The net force is leftward even while the cart moves right.

questions.prompt: Forces of 7 N and 11 N act rightward on a crate; a 5 N force acts leftward. Find the net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Group the forces pointing in the same direction.
Add the two rightward forces, then subtract the leftward force.
Calculate 7 + 11 − 5.

questions.prompt: An object moves left at constant nonzero velocity in an inertial frame. What is its net force?
hints: A continuing velocity does not require a continuing net push.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart has horizontal forces of 18 N right and 6 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: Add the forces before applying the second law.
Divide the net force by mass.
Calculate (18 − 6)/3.

questions.prompt: The mass doubles while the net force stays the same. What happens to acceleration?
hints: Keep the numerator fixed in a = F_net/m.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acceleration is net force divided by mass, so twice the mass gives half the acceleration.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart experiences a net force of 24 N rightward. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: The stated force is already the net force.
Use acceleration = net force divided by mass.
Divide the stated net force by the cart's mass.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving right has forces of 4 N right and 12 N left. With right positive, find its acceleration in m/s².
hints: The velocity does not change the force sum.
Subtract the leftward force and divide by mass.
Calculate (4 − 12)/4.

questions.prompt: What net force magnitude in newtons gives a 4 kg object an acceleration magnitude of 3 m/s²?
hints: This time, the mass and acceleration are known.
Multiply them to find net force.
Calculate 4 × 3.

questions.prompt: A heavier cart and a lighter cart must have the same acceleration. Which needs the larger net force?
hints: Hold acceleration fixed in the second law.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For a fixed acceleration, F_net = ma grows with mass.

choices.label: Both need the same net force

questions.prompt: An object has mass 3 kg where g = 10 m/s². Find the magnitude of its weight in newtons.
hints: Weight is a force produced by gravity.
Multiply mass by the stated gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 3 × 10.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object moves to a location with smaller gravitational acceleration. What happens to its mass?
hints: Mass and weight measure different physical quantities.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the gravitational field changes weight; the object's mass remains 3 kg.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object rests on a horizontal support. Only weight and the upward support force act, with g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: At rest, the vertical net force is zero.
The two vertical forces must have equal magnitudes.
Calculate the weight 4 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no vertical acceleration, support balances weight: N = 4 × 10 = 40 N.

questions.prompt: A support accelerates a 4 kg object upward at 2 m/s². Only support and weight act, and g = 10 m/s². Find the support force in newtons.
hints: The support must supply both weight balance and upward net force.
Use N = m(g + a).
Calculate 4 × (10 + 2).

questions.prompt: A 7 kg object is in a field where g = 9.8 m/s². Find its weight magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the given value of g rather than rounding it to 10.
Multiply mass by gravitational acceleration.
Calculate 7 × 9.8.

questions.prompt: An object on a support moves downward at constant velocity. Only weight and support act. How does the support force compare with weight?
hints: Downward velocity does not imply downward acceleration.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant velocity gives zero acceleration, so the support and weight balance.

questions.prompt: B pushes A left with a force of 10 N. Find the magnitude of A's force on B in newtons.
hints: Identify the two objects in the interaction.
The two forces have equal magnitudes.
The partner force has the same magnitude and opposite direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Newton's third law gives an equal magnitude: 10 N, directed right.

questions.prompt: Cart A pushes a 5 kg cart B right with 10 N. This is B's only horizontal force. Find B's acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Apply the second law to B alone.
Divide the force on B by B's mass.
Divide the interaction force by B's mass.

questions.prompt: Cart A has mass 2 kg. Its only horizontal force is 10 N left. With right positive, find A's acceleration in m/s².
hints: Use the mass of the object being accelerated.
The leftward force has a negative sign.
Divide the leftward force magnitude by mass and retain its sign.

questions.prompt: A and B push each other while isolated horizontally. Why do the interaction forces cancel in the combined system's force sum?
hints: Choose a boundary containing both interacting objects.

acceptedIdeas: They are equal, opposite internal forces
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For the combined system, the pair is internal and sums to zero. Each cart can still accelerate.

choices.label: They act on the same cart
They are equal, opposite internal forces

questions.prompt: Two carts interact with forces of magnitude 18 N. Cart B has mass 6 kg and no other horizontal force. Find its acceleration magnitude in m/s².
hints: Use the force acting on B.
Equal interaction forces do not require equal accelerations.
Divide the force magnitude by the mass of B.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which is the interaction partner of the table's upward force on the book?
hints: A third-law pair acts on different objects.

acceptedIdeas: The book's downward force on the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The paired force swaps the two objects: book on table, opposite to table on book.

choices.label: Earth's downward gravitational force on the book
The book's downward force on the table

questions.prompt: A resting 4 kg box has g = 10 m/s² and static coefficient 0.5. A 12 N horizontal push does not move it. Find the static-friction magnitude in newtons.
hints: A stationary box has zero horizontal acceleration.
Static friction adjusts below its maximum.
Match the applied horizontal push without exceeding the limit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 12 N push is below the 20 N limit, so static friction is 12 N.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box rests on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces. Use g = 10 m/s² and μ_s = 0.5. Find maximum static friction in newtons.
hints: First find the support force.
Multiply mg by the static coefficient.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 10.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box slides on a horizontal surface. With g = 10 m/s², no vertical acceleration and μ_k = 0.3, find the sliding-friction magnitude in newtons.
hints: Use the coefficient for sliding.
The support force equals mg.
Calculate 0.3 × 40.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box slides right. A 24 N push acts right and sliding friction is 12 N left. Find its acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Combine the opposing horizontal forces.
Divide net force by mass.
Calculate (24 − 12)/4.

questions.prompt: A stationary box can sustain at most 30 N of static friction. You push horizontally with 8 N and it stays at rest. What is its friction magnitude?
hints: Use zero acceleration while the box remains at rest.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Static friction balances the 8 N push; 30 N is a limit, not its automatic value.

questions.prompt: A sliding box slows to rest on a horizontal floor after its push is removed. What happens next in this model?
hints: Friction opposes sliding or a tendency to slide; it is not a constant backward motor.

acceptedIdeas: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once sliding stops and no horizontal force tries to move it, friction is zero.

choices.label: It stays at rest with zero horizontal friction
It keeps sliding at a smaller constant speed

questions.prompt: A constant 15 N force acts along a 4 m displacement. Find its work in joules.
hints: Force and displacement point the same way.
Multiply their magnitudes.
Calculate 15 × 4.

questions.prompt: A constant 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its signed work in joules.
hints: An opposing force does negative work.
Multiply force and distance, retaining the negative sign.
Calculate −6 × 5.

questions.prompt: A constant 20 N upward support force acts during a 3 m horizontal displacement. Find the work done by this support force in joules.
hints: Look for the force component along displacement.
The vertical force has no horizontal component.
A zero component gives zero work.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The force is perpendicular to displacement, so its work is 0 J.

questions.prompt: A constant 10 N pull acts along a 7 m displacement. Find the work done by this pull alone in joules.
hints: The question asks about one force, not the net force.
Use W = Fd for this parallel pull.
Calculate 10 × 7.

questions.prompt: You hold a box stationary for 5 s. What mechanical work does your support force do on the box during that time?
hints: Mechanical work depends on displacement, not the duration of effort.

acceptedIdeas: Zero work because displacement is zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The box has no displacement, so this support force does zero mechanical work on it.

choices.label: Zero work because displacement is zero

questions.prompt: A pull does +70 J on a cart and friction does −28 J. All other forces do zero work. What is the net work?
hints: Add work contributions with their signs.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is the signed sum: 70 − 28 = 42 J.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Kinetic energy uses speed squared.
Use K = ½mv².
Square the speed, multiply by mass, then take half.

questions.prompt: A cart's speed doubles while its mass stays fixed. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
hints: Keep the mass fixed.
Compare (2v)² with v².
Square the factor 2.

questions.prompt: A cart's mass doubles while its speed stays fixed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
hints: Separate the first power of mass from the square of speed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mass enters K = ½mv² as a direct multiplier, so energy doubles.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on it in joules.
hints: Calculate the final and initial kinetic energies.
Net work equals their difference.
Calculate 25 − 9.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object moves at speed 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Square speed before multiplying.
Use the one-half factor.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 25.

questions.prompt: A cart initially has 50 J of kinetic energy and comes to rest. What net work is done on it?
hints: Use the energy change, including its sign.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50 = −50 J.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object rises from 1 m to 5 m where g = 10 m/s². Find its gravitational potential-energy change in joules.
hints: Use the difference between final and initial height.
Multiply that difference by mg.
Calculate 3 × 10 × 4.

questions.prompt: You shift the zero-height reference while describing the same physical rise. What happens to its gravitational potential-energy change?
hints: Only the height difference enters ΔU.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both endpoint heights shift equally, leaving both Δh and ΔU unchanged.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find its signed gravitational potential-energy change in joules.
hints: Final height is less than initial height.
Use final minus initial height.
Calculate 2 × 10 × (−5).

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object descends from 8 m to 3 m with g = 10 m/s². Find the work done by gravity in joules.
hints: Gravity and this displacement point the same way.
Gravity's work is minus the potential-energy change.
Multiply the weight magnitude by the downward distance.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object rises by 1.5 m where g = 10 m/s². Find its gravitational potential-energy increase in joules.
hints: The height change is already given.
Multiply mass, g and height change.
Calculate 4 × 10 × 1.5.

questions.prompt: You assign U = 0 at the floor. Does an object at the floor necessarily have zero kinetic energy?
hints: Height and speed determine different forms of energy.

acceptedIdeas: No, it may still be moving
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The potential-energy reference says nothing about the object's speed or kinetic energy.

choices.label: Yes, all its energy must be zero
No, it may still be moving
Yes, because its height is zero

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object starts from rest at height 10 m with g = 10 m/s². It reaches zero height with no heating or other energy transfers. Find its final kinetic energy in joules.
hints: The initial kinetic energy is zero.
Use the potential-energy decrease.
Calculate mgh = 2 × 10 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Initial potential energy is 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J; all becomes kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object starts from rest at height 10 m with g = 10 m/s². At zero height, 40 J has become thermal energy and no other transfers occurred. Find its final kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Start with 200 J of potential energy.
Include the stated thermal energy in the account.
Subtract 40 from 200.

questions.prompt: A descending object loses mechanical energy through friction. The system contains the object, Earth and track, with no external energy transfers. Which sum stays constant?
hints: Follow the energy into the track as well as the object.

acceptedIdeas: Kinetic plus gravitational potential plus thermal energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Including the thermal energy produced by friction closes the energy account.

choices.label: Kinetic plus gravitational potential plus thermal energy

questions.prompt: A 2 kg object has final kinetic energy 100 J after a descent. Find its speed in m/s.
hints: Rearrange K = ½mv².
First calculate v² = 2K/m.
Take the square root of 100.

questions.prompt: An object starts with 12 J of kinetic energy, loses 90 J of gravitational potential energy and produces 18 J of thermal energy. No other transfers occur. Find its final kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Include the energy of motion already present.
Add the potential-energy decrease and subtract heating.
Calculate 12 + 90 − 18.

questions.prompt: With friction, which statement follows for a closed object-Earth-track system?
hints: Distinguish mechanical energy from all the energy forms inside the boundary.

acceptedIdeas: Mechanical energy can decrease while total energy stays constant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mechanical energy may become thermal energy while the total is conserved.

choices.label: Mechanical energy can decrease while total energy stays constant

questions.prompt: A device delivers 1,200 J of useful energy in 4 s. Find its average useful output power in watts.
hints: Power measures energy per unit time.
Divide useful energy by the interval.
Calculate 1,200/4.

questions.prompt: A device takes in 2,000 J and delivers 1,200 J as useful energy over the same interval. Find its efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Compare useful output with input.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
Calculate 100 × 0.6.

questions.prompt: A device takes in 2,000 J, provides 1,200 J of useful output and stores no net energy. How many joules leave through its other outputs?
hints: Account for all the input energy.
Subtract useful output from input.
Calculate 2,000 − 1,200.

questions.prompt: A machine delivers the same useful energy in half the time. What happens to its average useful output power?
hints: Keep the energy fixed while changing the denominator.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: P = E/t doubles when E stays fixed and t halves.

questions.prompt: A device delivers 350 J of useful output from 500 J input. Find its efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Place useful output in the numerator.
Divide by input, then multiply by 100.
Calculate 100 × 0.7.

questions.prompt: A device is claimed to deliver more total output energy than all its input energy, with no decrease in stored energy. What must be checked?
hints: Draw the system boundary and account for every energy transfer.

acceptedIdeas: Missing inputs, storage changes or incorrect measurements
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy conservation requires all inputs, outputs and storage changes to balance.

choices.label: Only the rate of useful energy delivery
Missing inputs, storage changes or incorrect measurements
Only the fraction of output labelled useful

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart moves right at 4 m/s. With right positive, find its momentum in kg·m/s.
hints: Momentum is mass times signed velocity.
Use positive velocity for rightward motion.
Calculate 3 × 4.

questions.prompt: A constant net force of 6 N right acts for 3 s. With right positive, find the impulse in N·s.
hints: Impulse combines net force and its duration.
Multiply force by time.
Calculate 6 × 3.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart initially moves right at 4 m/s. A net impulse of +18 N·s acts. With right positive, find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Start with the initial momentum.
Add impulse before dividing by mass.
Calculate (12 + 18)/3.

questions.prompt: A cart reverses from +4 m/s to −4 m/s without changing mass. Which endpoint quantity is unchanged?
hints: Compare how velocity enters p = mv and K = ½mv².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The speed squared is unchanged, so kinetic energy is the same; momentum and velocity reverse signs.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moving at +6 m/s stops in 3 s. Find the average net force in newtons with right positive.
hints: Stopping reduces the positive momentum to zero.
Divide the signed momentum change by time.
Divide the lost momentum by the stopping time and retain its negative sign.

questions.prompt: The same object undergoes the same momentum change over a longer stopping time. What happens to the magnitude of its average net force?
hints: Use F_avg = Δp/Δt with a fixed numerator.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed impulse is spread over more time, reducing average force magnitude.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart and they stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.
hints: Add both initial signed momenta.
The stuck carts have combined mass 6 kg.
Divide 12 by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total momentum is 2 × 6 + 4 × 0 = 12 kg·m/s; v = 12/(2 + 4) = 2 m/s.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s and a 4 kg cart at −3 m/s collide and stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.
hints: Include the negative sign of the second velocity.
Add 12 and −12.
Divide the total momentum by 6 kg.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Initial momentum is 2 × 6 + 4 × (−3) = 0; final velocity is 0 m/s.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart at 6 m/s hits a resting 4 kg cart. They stick and move at 2 m/s. How many joules of kinetic energy are converted into other forms?
hints: Calculate kinetic energy before and after contact.
Use the combined mass for the final state.
Subtract 12 J from 36 J.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Initial K = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J; final K = ½ × 6 × 2² = 12 J; decrease = 24 J.

questions.prompt: What condition justifies conserving the total momentum of two colliding carts?
hints: Separate internal collision forces from external influences.

acceptedIdeas: The external impulse on the two-cart system is negligible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The total momentum changes by external impulse, so negligible external impulse permits momentum conservation.

choices.label: The carts must have equal mass
The external impulse on the two-cart system is negligible
The carts must conserve kinetic energy

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart at +4 m/s hits a resting 1 kg cart and they stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find total initial momentum.
Use the combined mass after sticking.
Divide total initial momentum by the combined mass.

questions.prompt: In an isolated sticking collision, what is conserved across the collision?
hints: Apply the conservation rule to the whole system.

acceptedIdeas: Total momentum; kinetic energy may become other forms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Internal forces exchange momentum between carts; total momentum remains fixed while some kinetic energy becomes other forms.

choices.label: Total momentum; kinetic energy may become other forms
Kinetic energy, but not total momentum
